draft.title: Non-material living standards
card: Non-material living standards are the parts of wellbeing that money cannot buy directly. They are about quality of life, not the goods a person owns.
Examples include health, safety, freedom, a clean environment and leisure time, which is time free from work.
Money can help, for example by paying for a doctor. But a person cannot buy good health, safety or free time outright, and these are not counted as goods and services.
Two people with the same income can have different non-material living standards. One may work long hours in a polluted city, while the other has more free time and clean air.
draft.remember: Non-material living standards are about quality of life, which income alone does not decide.

a.q: Which of these is a non-material living standard?
opts: Having time free from work to spend with family
Owning a large house in a city suburb
Having a car and a modern phone
Earning a high wage from a full-time job
a.why: Leisure time is part of quality of life, and money cannot buy it directly. A house, a car and a wage are about goods and income, so they are material living standards.
a.clue: Which one is not something you can buy or earn?

b.q: Ravi and Tess earn the same wage. Ravi works 60 hours a week in a smoggy city. Tess works 35 hours a week in a town with clean air. What does this show?
opts: Equal income can leave non-material standards different
Tess has a higher income because her town is cleaner
Ravi has better material standards because he works more
Non-material standards depend only on hours worked
b.why: Their incomes match, but Tess has more leisure time and a cleaner environment, so her non-material living standards are higher. Working longer does not change Ravi's income here, and hours are only one part of non-material living standards.
b.clue: Compare their wages first, then compare their time and air.

a.best: Having time free from work to spend with family

b.best: Equal income can leave non-material standards different

problems.detail: 'Ravi and Tess earn the same wage' is ambiguous. In economics a wage is often an hourly rate, and at the same hourly rate Ravi's 60 hours would earn far more than Tess's 35. Read that way, 'Ravi has better material standards because he works more' becomes defensible. Say they earn the same weekly income, which is what the why assumes ('Their incomes match').

check.summary: The card, the remember line and question a are accurate. Question b should say Ravi and Tess earn the same weekly income, not the same wage, because the same hourly wage over more hours would give Ravi a higher income.
